analysis.one_liner: Caps prison phone rates, bans per-call fees, and ends kickback payments from phone companies to prisons.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 14 Democratic cosponsors, never received a hearing or a vote and died in the Energy and Commerce Committee when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Prison phone calls have long cost far more than ordinary calls — often more than a dollar a minute — because companies bid for exclusive jail contracts by paying 'site commissions' back to the facilities, which pushes rates up. This bill would have capped calls at 4 to 5 cents a minute, banned one-time connection fees and most add-on charges, and outlawed site commissions entirely. It would have required the FCC to set permanent maximum rates based on providers' actual costs, and applied the caps to existing contracts as well as new ones.
analysis.who_benefits: Families of the roughly two million people in U.S. jails and prisons — the grandparents, parents, and spouses who pay for the calls — most of them low-income. The bill's own findings describe a grandmother who had to choose between medication and calling her incarcerated grandson. Lower rates also benefit communities, since the findings note that staying in touch reduces recidivism.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families paying for calls to jailed loved ones

how_it_helps.text: Caps voice calls at $0.04 per minute for debit and prepaid calling and $0.05 per minute for collect calling until the FCC writes permanent rules.
Requires all charges to be assessed per minute for the actual call length and bans per-call and per-connection fees, which today can add more than the call itself costs.
Prohibits 'site commissions' — the payments phone companies make to prisons and jails to win contracts, which the bill's findings identify as the main reason rates are unjust and unreasonable.
Limits ancillary fees such as payment processing and live-agent fees, capping them at cost or modest fixed amounts.
Applies the new rules to existing provider contracts within 60 days and bars extending old contract terms, so current exclusive-deal arrangements could not lock in high rates.

analysis.who_pays: Prison telephone companies, whose revenues rest on above-cost rates and site commissions, and the state and local corrections agencies and private prison operators that receive those commissions as revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Prison phone companies and commission-receiving facilities

drawbacks.text: The bill set interim caps of $0.04–$0.05 per minute by statute, before the FCC completed a cost record, and requires permanent rates to be based on average industry costs — rates that low could strain providers' margins and their ability to fund security-validated phone and video systems.

Facilities use site-commission revenue to offset the cost of phone equipment, tablets, and in some cases inmate programs; ending the commissions removes that revenue stream and shifts those costs back to agencies and taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people who pay for prison calls — disproportionately low-income families — the savings are large and direct, and ending site commissions targets the actual cause of inflated rates, a distortion the bill's findings document at length. The honest cost is on the other side of the ledger: facility budgets and phone-system upgrades that were quietly funded out of call revenue would need replacement funding. On balance the bill attacked a genuine market failure — the buyer (the facility) profits from overcharging the actual customer (the family).

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee for the rest of the two-year Congress — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and died there on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush introduced the bill on March 25, 2020, naming it for Martha Wright-Reed, the grandmother who led a decade-long campaign for just prison phone rates after having to choose between medication and calling her grandson.
Fourteen House Democrats signed on as cosponsors; no Republican did.

The House referred the bill to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day it was introduced, and the committee took no further action on it for the remainder of the 116th Congress, which ended January 3, 2021.

The bill's findings state that the market is distorted because facilities choose phone providers based largely on which pays the biggest site commission, a cost passed on to families as unjust and unreasonable rates.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prison phone companies kept charging above-cost rates, and the facilities kept collecting site commissions — the practice the bill would have banned. The families paying for the calls gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Prison phone companies and commission-collecting facilities

for.name: Bobby L. Rush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Martha Wright Prison Phone Justice Act on March 25, 2020.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chairman, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or floor vote; it received no committee action after referral and expired at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Prison phone providers
against.role: Industry (firms such as Securus and Global Tel Link)
against.what_they_did: Opposed rate caps and commission bans, which would cut heavily into revenues built on above-cost calling rates and site commissions.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but no vote ever occurred, so the partisan split on the bill itself was never tested.

industries.note: These companies profit by charging families above-market rates — historically over $1 a minute plus per-call fees — secured through exclusive contracts. The bill would cap rates at a few cents per minute, ban connection fees and most add-on charges, and outlaw the site commissions used to win contracts.

industries.industry: State and local corrections agencies and private prison operators
industries.note: These entities receive site commissions from phone providers — a revenue stream the bill would end entirely. Their financial interest in bigger commissions ran directly against the families who pay for the calls.
